title: Rate law from initial rates, then an integrated rate law
promptMarkdown:
**Part A.** The gas-phase reaction $\ce{2 NO(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2 NOCl(g)}$ was studied at a fixed temperature. The initial-rate data below are constructed for this exercise (they are not measurements):

| Run | $[\ce{NO}]_0$ / M | $[\ce{Cl2}]_0$ / M | Initial rate / M s⁻¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.10 | 0.10 | $1.8\times10^{-4}$ |
| 2 | 0.20 | 0.10 | $7.2\times10^{-4}$ |
| 3 | 0.10 | 0.20 | $3.6\times10^{-4}$ |

Here 'rate' means $\tfrac12 d[\ce{NOCl}]/dt$.

1. Determine the order with respect to $\ce{NO}$ and to $\ce{Cl2}$, showing the ratio of rates you used for each.
2. Write the rate law and compute $k$ with its units.
3. Explain why the rate law could not have been read from the stoichiometric coefficients, and under what condition it could.

**Part B.** A different compound decomposes by a first-order process with $k = 2.50\times10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ at the temperature of the run.

4. Compute the half-life and the time for the concentration to fall to 10% of its initial value. State what, if anything, these times depend on besides $k$.
hintLadder: Compare runs that change one concentration only: runs 1 and 2 for $\ce{NO}$, runs 1 and 3 for $\ce{Cl2}$. The ratio of rates equals the ratio of concentrations raised to the order.
Once the orders are known, substitute any run into the rate law to solve for $k$, and work out its units from rate divided by the concentration factors.
For a first-order process, $\ln([\ce{A}]_t/[\ce{A}]_0) = -kt$; set the ratio to $\tfrac12$ and to $0.10$.

deterministicChecks.description: asserting first order in NO or second order in Cl2

criteria.criterion: Doubling [NO] quadruples the rate (second order in NO); doubling [Cl2] doubles it (first order in Cl2), with the ratios shown.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Both orders with the ratio argument.

criteria.criterion: Orders are experimental and equal the coefficients only for an elementary step; the termolecular appearance here is a coincidence of this data set, not evidence of mechanism.
t½ = ln 2/k = 277 s; t(10%) = ln 10/k = 921 s; both independent of the initial concentration for first order.

levels.label: met
levels.description: Both times and the independence statement.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Times right, independence missing, or one time wrong.

checkExamples.label: correct answer
checkExamples.text: Runs 1 and 2: [NO] doubles and the rate goes from 1.8e-4 to 7.2e-4, a factor of 4 = 2^2, so second order in NO. Runs 1 and 3: [Cl2] doubles and the rate doubles, first order in Cl2. Rate = k[NO]^2[Cl2]; k = 1.8e-4/(0.10^2 x 0.10) = 0.18 M^-2 s^-1. The orders are experimental; they would equal the coefficients only if the reaction were a single elementary (here termolecular) step, which the data alone cannot establish. Part B: t1/2 = 0.693/2.50e-3 = 277 s; t(10%) = ln(10)/2.50e-3 = 921 s; neither depends on the initial concentration.

checkExamples.label: orders read from coefficients
checkExamples.text: From the equation the reaction is second order in NO and first order in Cl2... actually I get first order in NO from runs 1 and 2 since the rate increases. k = 0.018. t1/2 = 400 s.

difficulty.basis: Ratios of initial rates for two orders, k with units from one run, and two first-order times from ln 2/k and ln 10/k; the lesson works the same steps on other numbers.
